title: Headroom credit ledger and failover lanes — Dedicated capacity PRD (WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD to propose the "headroom credit ledger" and "failover lanes" features for Redwood Dedicated capacity. The goal is a pragmatic autoscaling and burst model that preserves tenant isolation while enabling short-lived capacity overcommit for latency-sensitive workloads. This doc focuses on product requirements, guardrails, operational signals, and rollout strategy.

Problem statement / motivating examples:
- Customer A runs a chat service with mostly predictable baseline traffic but periodic end-of-quarter spikes. They want bounded, cheap bursts without losing isolation guarantees for other tenants.
- Customer B needs firm latency SLO for API requests and will accept occasional soft throttling instead of expensive reserved scale-ups.
- Today, dedicated capacity is either static (reserved) or uses coarse autoscaling resulting in either wasted reserve or noisy neighbour incidents during spikes. We need a mechanism that:
  - Lets tenants consume limited extra capacity when available,
  - Ensures critical tenants are protected from others’ bursts,
  - Provides predictable cost attribution and clear operational behavior.

High level approach / concepts:
1) Headroom credit ledger (HCL): a per-tenancy account of "burst credits" that can be consumed when a tenant exceeds their reserved baseline. Credits are earned by:
   - unused reserved capacity over time (accrual),
   - manual top-ups from a billing action or support,
   - credit transfers for emergencies (admin action).
   - credits decay after 30 days by default (configurable).
2) Failover lanes (FL): pre-authorized, soft preemptible worker lanes (GPU slots or CPU nodes) that can be used for short bursts. Lanes have:
   - priority buckets (gold/silver/bronze) mapped to isolation policies,
   - eviction policies (preempt to protect higher-priority customers),
   - a configurable max duration per request or session to prevent indefinite use.
3) Isolation score & guardrails: a lightweight runtime computed score per tenant that considers
   - historical steal-rate (how often they caused preemption),
   - ratio of credits used to baseline, and
   - SLO tier (enterprise vs self-serve).
  The platform will reduce burst eligibility for tenants with poor isolation scores.

Product requirements (user-facing):
- API/console:
  - Enable/disable "Dynamic Headroom" per dedicated pool.
  - Show current credits, accrual rate, recent consumption, and projected days until refill.
  - Button to purchase/top-up credits (billing flow out-of-scope, stubbed).
  - View per-tenant failover lane history (evictions, durations).
- Behavioral guarantees:
  - When credits remain and failover lanes are available, requests may be routed to lanes with a clear priority label.
  - If lane capacity is exhausted, requests are either queued within configured latency-bound queues or fallback to a cheaper model variant per the tenant’s policy.
  - Eviction must be signaled with a 409-style error (or streaming close) and a structured reason for SDKs to surface.
- Billing/attribution:
  - Additional token cost for using failover lanes will be reported separately in billing exports.
  - Credits consumed should be visible in Cost API and Console reports.

Operational / runtime requirements:
- Autoscaler integration: HCL should be consulted before autoscaler spins new reserved instances. Failover lanes are independent short-lived allocations created from a separate pool.
- Telemetry: emit these signals at per-request granularity:
  - headroom_credit_change (+/-), headroom_balance, headroom_accrual_rate
  - failover_lane_assigned (lane_id, priority), failover_evicted (evict_reason)
  - isolation_score, lane_wait_time_ms, queue_time_ms
- Safety circuit breakers:
  - Global: platform-wide threshold that disables all failover lanes if system utilization > 92% to avoid mass preemption cascades.
  - Pool-level: if a dedicated pool's eviction rate > 2% over 10 minutes, throttle new lane assignments and notify SRE.
  - Tenant-level: if a tenant’s eviction_count > 5 in 24h, reduce their headroom accrual rate by 50% until manual review.

Configuration model (example snippets):
- Pool config (console / API):
  {
    "pool_id": "dp-west-01",
    "dynamic_headroom_enabled": true,
    "lane_pool_size": 20,
    "lane_priorities": ["gold","silver","bronze"],
    "global_safety_threshold": 0.92
  }
- Tenant policy (example):
  {
    "tenant_id": "acct-123",
    "baseline_reserved": 4,
    "max_burst_concurrency": 8,
    "credit_accrual_rate": "0.5 credits/hour",
    "fallback_route": "model-variant:fast-lt"
  }

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Noisy neighbour incidents (measured as >10ms median p95 latency increase for protected tenants) reduced by 60% in early trials.
- Mean time to detect preemption cascades < 2 minutes after rollout.
- 80% of eligible burst requests served from failover lanes when credits are available.
- Accurate billing: credits consumed show up in daily billing export within 24h.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Alpha: internal-only, two pools, simulate credit accrual and lane assignment using canary traffic. (2–4 weeks)
- Beta: selected customers opt-in (industrial & fintech customers), add console views and billing integration. Monitor isolation score and eviction rates closely. (6–8 weeks)
- Gradual rollout: 10% of pools, automated rollback if pool-level eviction_rate > threshold. (4–6 weeks)
- GA: make feature opt-out for Reserved customers, docs & runbook published. (TBD)

Operational playbooks (high level):
- On detection of pool-level preemption cascade:
  1) Disable lane assignment for the pool.
  2) Increase autoscaler weight to spin reserved instances where possible.
  3) Notify SRE and affected customers with template message.
- Tenant appeals: support can manually adjust headroom balance and isolation score; all adjustments require an audit log entry.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Credit semantics: should credits be based on tokens consumed, vCPU/GPU seconds, or request-count? (tokens ties directly to billing but is expensive to compute real-time)
- Duration enforcement: enforce per-request max time or per-connection? Long-running streaming sessions complicate lane eviction.
- Preemptible pricing: how to price lane time vs reserved? Flat multiplier vs dynamic spot-style pricing?
- Cross-pool failover: should failover lanes be shared across pools in the same region or strictly per-pool? Shared lanes increase efficiency but complicate isolation.

Risks / mitigations:
- Risk: mispriced burst lanes leads to revenue leakage. Mitigation: walled-garden beta with manual billing verification.
- Risk: eviction storm when many tenants concurrently consume credits. Mitigation: global safety circuit breaker and soft backpressure queueing.
- Risk: complexity for customers understanding credits. Mitigation: clear console UI, projected-day visual, and sample calculators in docs.

Next steps / immediate TODOs:
- Engineering spike (infra): prototype HCL store and per-request hook to debit/credit (owner: Miguel) — 2 weeks.
- SRE: define observability dashboard (owner: Jules) — 1 week.
- Product: finalize API contract and console mockups (owner: Samira) — 2 weeks.
- Billing: design export schema and one-off top-up flow (owner: Asha) — 2 weeks.

Appendix: example operator CLI commands (sketch)
- Check tenant balance: rwctl headroom get acct-123 --pool dp-west-01
- Top up credits: rwctl headroom topup acct-123 --amount 10 --reason "emergency"
- Disable lanes: rwctl pool set dp-west-01 --dynamic-headroom false
